title: Dahi Wale Tinde: The Yogurt Curry That Makes Humble Tinda Irresistible
excerpt: This North Indian summer staple transforms the often-dismissed apple gourd into a tangy, spiced yogurt curry that pairs perfectly with roti or paratha.
body:
• Dahi wale tinde is a North Indian yogurt-based curry featuring apple gourd (tinda), a seasonal summer vegetable
  • The dish uses whisked yogurt tempered with spices to transform tinda's mild flavor into something rich and tangy
  • Shallow-frying tinda pieces before adding them to the curry removes rawness and adds texture
  • The recipe takes about 30 minutes and serves 4, making it ideal for weeknight dinners at home

Tinda — the small, round apple gourd that shows up in Indian kitchens every summer — doesn't exactly inspire excitement. Children push it around their plates. Adults tolerate it. But dahi wale tinde, a yogurt-simmered preparation popular across North India, might be the dish that finally changes tinda's reputation.

The recipe, which has been circulating widely on Indian food platforms this week, takes a vegetable most people consider bland and coats it in a spiced yogurt gravy that's tangy, aromatic, and deeply satisfying. As one Aaj Tak food feature put it, once you try this version, "even paneer and rich curries will seem bland by comparison."

What Makes This Dish Work

The secret lies in how the yogurt is handled. Fresh dahi is whisked with turmeric, red chilli powder, and coriander powder before it ever touches the pan. This pre-mixing prevents the yogurt from splitting when it hits the heat — a common pitfall that turns many dahi-based curries grainy.

The tinda pieces themselves get a quick shallow fry in mustard oil before joining the curry. This step, often skipped in simpler preparations, removes the raw, slightly bitter edge that puts people off the vegetable. The fried pieces develop a light golden exterior that holds up well in the gravy without turning to mush.

"The bland taste of tinda gets a new makeover with yogurt and pickling spices."

— Banaras Ka Khana food blog

The Full Method

Start with about 400-500 grams of tinda, peeled and cut into medium pieces. Heat 2-3 tablespoons of mustard oil (or any neutral oil) in a kadai and shallow-fry the tinda until lightly golden. Set them aside.

In the same pan, temper cumin seeds and asafoetida, then add ginger-garlic paste and fry briefly. Add finely chopped onion and cook until golden. Follow with chopped tomato and salt, cooking until the tomato breaks down and releases oil.

Turn the heat to its lowest setting. Pour in the whisked yogurt-spice mixture and stir constantly — this is the critical step. Keep stirring until the masala separates and the raw smell of the spices disappears. Add the fried tinda, coat everything well, and splash in 2-3 tablespoons of water for a thick, clinging gravy.

Cover and simmer on low heat for 7-10 minutes until the tinda is tender all the way through. Finish with garam masala, crushed kasuri methi (dried fenugreek leaves), and fresh coriander. Serve hot with chapati or paratha.

Ingredients at a Glance

The pantry list is straightforward: tinda (400g), half a cup of whisked yogurt, one large onion, one tomato, ginger-garlic paste, cumin, asafoetida, turmeric, Kashmiri red chilli powder, coriander powder, garam masala, kasuri methi, mustard oil, fresh coriander, and salt. Some variations from Archana's Kitchen add gram flour (besan) to the yogurt mixture, which thickens the gravy further and adds a subtle nuttiness. Fenugreek seeds and mustard seeds in the tempering give the dish a more pronounced North Indian character.

A Seasonal Staple Worth Rediscovering

Tinda's growing season runs from late spring through the monsoon months, making it one of the most affordable vegetables available in Indian markets right now. A kilo rarely costs more than ₹30-40 in most cities. For the diaspora, tinda can be harder to find — Indian grocery stores in the US, UK, and Canada stock it seasonally, typically between June and September. When it's unavailable, some cooks substitute zucchini or chayote, though neither replicates tinda's particular soft, spongy texture that absorbs curry so well.

The dish belongs to a broader tradition of dahi-based sabzis — yogurt curries — that are central to North Indian vegetarian cooking. Dahi bhindi, dahi aloo, and dahi baingan all follow similar logic: a mild vegetable elevated by spiced, tempered yogurt. What distinguishes the tinda version is how completely the gourd absorbs the surrounding flavors, becoming almost a vehicle for the curry itself.

For home cooks looking to break out of the paneer-and-dal rotation, dahi wale tinde offers something genuinely different: a 30-minute dish that costs almost nothing to make but delivers restaurant-level depth. It's the kind of everyday Indian cooking that deserves more attention — especially from those of us who grew up dismissing tinda as boring.
